title: Statistical methods to analyze the persistence of threatened birds using citizen science data
author: Udani Wijewardhana
license_note: Confirmed via CrossRef DOI metadata: dx.doi.org/10.17504/protocols.io.3c8gizw

6 Results This review refers to studies conducted between 1727 to 2017 in 10 different countries, with more than one country providing the data for some of the articles (Boakes, Isaac, Fuller, Mace & McGowan 2018; Wilson, Anderson, Wilson, Bertram & Arcese 2013; Studds et al., 2017; Yong et al., 2017 ). The highest number of studies was carri ed out in the United States of America (12) and Africa (7), followed by the East Asian–Australasian Flyway (3), Canada (3), Australia (2). Due to the variability in the included studies in terms of study design, sample size, persistence or extinction risk, objectives and statistical methods for analysing the data, this systematic review will provide a qualitative review, rather than a meta-analysis. Approximately half (49%) of studies were discussed only a single bird species such as Carnaby's cockatoo (Calyptorhynchus latirostris), Aransas -Wood Buffalo Whooping cranes (Grus americana), Western Grebes ( Aechmophorus occidentalis), Black Harrier ( Circus maurus), Western capercaillie (Tetrao urogallus) . Group studies of species were used for the remaining studies; for example, forest pigeons, North American quails, breeding species of Chinese protected birds, most abundant migratory shorebirds. In these 37 papers, citizen science data were analysed using more than 10 different statistical models and these models can be categorized into four categories. A summary of the statistical methods grouped under these categories are listed below. (a) Generalised linear models (32%) including General linear models, Generalised additive models, Poisson regression models, ANOVA, logistic regression models and least square regression model (Pearse et al., 2018; Erickson, Found -Jackson & Boyce 2017; Dhanjal‐
Adams et al., 2019; Carvalho et al., 2014; Downs, Pfeiffer & Hart 2014; Pryke, Samways & Hockey 2010; Shaw, Jenkins, Allan & Ryan 2015; Kamp, Koshkin & Sheldon 2009; Amar & Cloete 2017; Aubry, Desrochers & Seutin 2016 ; Yong et al., 2017; Xu et al., 2019). (b) Machine learning models (24%) including predictive models, maximum entropy models, boosted regression trees (BRT), random forests (RF), clustering models (Ramesh, Gopalakrishna, Barve & Melnick 2017; Rösner, S., Brandl, Segelbacher, Lorenc, & Müller 2014; KrÓLikowska, KrupiŃSki & KuczyŃSki 2017; Zlonis, Panci, Bednar, Hamady & Niemi 2017; Wogan, 2016; Tanner, Papeş, Elmore, Fuhlendorf & Davis 2017; Li et al., 2015; Hart, Kelly & Pearson 2018; Runge, Tulloch, Hammill, Possingham & Fuller 2015). (c) Linear mixed/Hierarchical models (2 2%) including general linear mixed models, mixed effects cumulative logit regression model, hierarchical mixed effect model (Garcia-Heras et al., 2019; Wilson, Anderson, Wilson, Bertram & Arcese 2013; Rushing, Dudash, Studds & Marra 2015; Berry, Benkman, Muela, Seminario & Curti 2010; Wilson, Smith, Naujokaitis-Lewis & McCarthy 2018; Studds et al., 2017; Thogmartin, Sauer & Knutson 2004; Clemens et al., 2016). (d) Miscellaneous (22%) including deterministic model, models for occupancy, persistence model, stage structure matrix model and count-based population viability analysis (Williams, Yates, Saunders, Dawson & Barrett 2017; Lee, Altwegg & Barnard 2017; Boakes, Isaac, Fuller , Mace & McGowan 2018; Ward et al., 2015; Kalle, Ramesh & Downs 2018; Erickson, Found -Jackson & Boyce 2014; Wootton & Bell, 2014 ; Culp, Cohen, Scarpignato, Thogmartin, & Marra 2017).

steps.title: Define Search Strategy and Databases
steps.instruction: Develop individualized search strategies for the Web of Science, Scopus, and ProQuest Central databases to identify journal articles published between January 1900 and January 2019 in English.

substeps.instruction: Use Web of Science query: (TS=("bird*") AND TS=("threatened” OR “endangered” or “vulnerable”) AND TS=(“citizen science”) AND TS=(“persistence” OR “extinction risk”) AND TS=("statistic*" OR "statistical model*" OR quantitative OR “Models, Statistical” OR trend* OR "predictive model*")) AND LANGUAGE: (English)

Use Scopus query: ( "bird*" ) AND ( "threatened" OR "endangered" OR "vulnerable" ) AND ( "citizen science" ) AND ( "persistence" OR "extinction risk" ) AND ( "statistic*" OR "statistical model*" OR "Models,Statistical" OR "trend*" OR "predictive model*" ) AND ( LIMIT-TO ( SRCTYPE , "j" ) ) AND ( LIMIT TO ( LANGUAGE , "English" ) )

Use ProQuest Central query: ((bird*) AND ((threatened) OR (endangered) OR (vulnerable)) AND (citizen science) AND ((persistence) OR (extinction risk)) AND ((statistic*) OR (statistical model*) OR (Models, Statistical) OR (trend*) OR (predictive model*))) AND la.exact("ENG") AND PEER( yes) AND stype.exact("Scholarly Journals")

steps.title: Apply Inclusion and Exclusion Criteria
steps.instruction: Screen identified articles based on four specific inclusion criteria to ensure alignment with the study objective.

substeps.instruction: Verify the study focuses on threatened bird species under IUCN red list assessment criteria, or species in near threatened/least concern categories that are declining in population/range.
Confirm that Citizen Science data were used to conduct the study.
Ensure the study discusses persistence or extinction risk of threatened bird species.
Confirm the study performed quantitative analysis using statistical modelling, predictive modelling, or trend analysis.

steps.title: Execute Selection and Data Extraction Process
steps.instruction: Manage the identified literature through a systematic screening and deduplication process.

substeps.instruction: Upload all identified articles to EndNote software.
Remove duplicate articles (performed by the first author).
Independently screen titles and abstracts against inclusion criteria (performed by the first two authors).
Direct articles with questionable eligibility to a third reviewer for resolution.
Perform a full-text review of the shortlisted articles to determine the final set for inclusion.

steps.title: Perform Quality Assessment
steps.instruction: Assess the quality of the included articles using the 'Udani DM Checklist', which is based on the Downs and Black checklist.

substeps.instruction: Evaluate the 22 items across five sub-scales: reporting (9 items), external validity (4 items), internal validity-bias (4 items), internal validity-confounding (4 items), and power (1 item).
Score each item as '1' for compliance and '0' for non-compliance.
Calculate the standard deviation for each item to check discrimination capability.
Categorize the total score: low quality (10-13), fair quality (14-15), average quality (16-18), and high quality (19-22).

steps.title: Classify Statistical Techniques and Data
steps.instruction: Categorize the included articles based on the statistical methods, data types, and risk factors identified, using the 'guide for choosing among statistical techniques' (Tabachnick & Fidell, 2013).

substeps.instruction: Classify statistical methods into categories: general linear models, machine learning models, linear mixed/hierarchical models, or miscellaneous.
Classify citizen science data source as either Database data or Survey data.
Classify the nature of survey data as either Abundance data or Presence-absence data.
Categorize risk factors as Biotic (e.g., habitat loss, climate change) or Abiotic (e.g., hunting, agriculture intensification).

description: 2 Introduction About 10 years ago, two scientists decided to estimate the total number of birds on the planet. The number they came up with was 200 to 400 billion individual birds. Since the 1500s, birds have been declining both in terms of species numbers (by about 500 species) and numbers of individuals (by about 20-25%) (How big is the bird population? | AMNH. (n.d.)) . Due to risk factors such as climate change, habitat destruction, changes to wetlands and coastal environments, predation by feral predators, overhunting, toxic pollution and ecological change (whether these are caused by natural or man -made influences), bird extinctions are now occurring at a rate that far exceeds their speciation rate. Each extinction diminishes the diversity and complexity of life on earth (Fws.gov., 2018). The world's tropical forest bird population is estimated to be permanently reduced by 144 million individuals per year. Of all the known bird species, 129 are extinct and out of the remaining 9,787 1,313 bird species are threatened with extinction according to BirdLife International’s assessment for the 2012 IUCN Red List. Of these, 197 are considered Critically Endangered and are on the brink of extinction (Butchart, S., 2013). By the year 2100, up to 14% of all bird species may become extinct, and 7-25% (28-56% on oceanic islands) may become "functionally extinct", in the sense that the number of individuals within these species will become so low that the species will no longer play an important role in their ecosystem (How big is the bird population? | AMNH. (n.d.)). Birds play a vital role in ecosystems. For example, birds pollinate and disperse the seeds of many plants, including many crops important to humans. They are also helpful in controlling crop pests. Scavenger birds such as vultures help with the decomposition of organic material (How big is the bird population? | AMNH. (n.d.)). When a bird species is lost, the benefits it might have afforded are gone forever
